# Nevus

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric dermatology > Nevus*

[Original Article Link](/library/6k0jKT)

---

## Summary

Nevi are congenital or acquired benign <u>neoplasms</u> of the <u>skin</u> that are classified as either melanocytic or <u>epidermal</u>. Melanocytic nevi (moles) are composed of pigment-producing nevus cells derived from <u>melanocytes</u> and can manifest in multiple forms (e.g., <u>common acquired melanocytic nevus</u>, <u>atypical nevus</u>, <u>Spitz nevus</u>). <u>Epidermal nevi</u> are cutaneous <u>hamartomas</u> caused by <u>hyperplasia</u> of the <u>epidermis</u> and/or adnexa that typically manifest at <u>birth</u> or during early childhood, and occur either as an isolated lesion (e.g., <u>nevus sebaceous</u>, <u>inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus</u>, and <u>Becker nevus</u>) or with extracutaneous abnormalities (i.e., <u>epidermal nevus syndrome</u>). Careful <u>history taking</u> and <u>skin examination</u> are required to differentiate between the types of nevi. If there is concern for <u>malignancy</u> (e.g., <u>ABCDE criteria</u>, <u>ugly duckling sign</u>, <u>clinical features of BCC</u>) or <u>Spitz nevus</u>, a <u>skin biopsy</u> is necessary. Individuals with a suspected <u>epidermal nevus syndrome</u> require further evaluation and management by a specialist. All individuals with histologic confirmation of <u>malignancy</u> should be treated accordingly; see also “<u>Treatment of BCC</u>” and “<u>Treatment of melanoma</u>.” Otherwise, treatment is generally unnecessary unless desired for cosmetic reasons.




<u>Congenital melanocytic nevus</u> and <u>congenital dermal melanocytosis</u> are discussed elsewhere.

## Melanocytic nevus

### Overview [[1]](/library/lPWvUl0)[[2]](/library/Wk1P5S0)




* Melanocytic nevus (mole) is a benign cutaneous <u>tumor</u> composed of pigment-producing nevus cells derived from <u>melanocytes</u>.

* <u>Histopathology</u>: well-nested melanocytic proliferations at the <u>dermal-epidermal junction</u>





| Overview of melanocytic nevi (moles) |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Atypical nevus</u> | <u>Common acquired melanocytic nevus</u> | <u>Spitz nevus</u> |
| <u>Epidemiology</u> | <br>* Northern European descent, light <u>hair</u>, and <u>freckles</u><br><br> | <br>* Common regardless of age, <u>gender</u>, or ethnicity<br><br> | <br>* More common in children<br><br> |
| Clinical features | <br>* Appearance is similar to <u>melanomas</u>, i.e., <u>ABCDE criteria</u>.   [[3]](/library/07We450)[[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)<br><br> | <br>* Vary by stage (junctional nevus, <u>compound nevus</u>, and <u>dermal</u> nevus)<br><br> | <br>* Solitary, dome-shaped <u>papule</u> or <u>nodule</u> that appears suddenly<br><br> |
| Management | <br><br>* If <u>melanoma</u> is suspected, perform a <u>full-thickness excisional biopsy</u>.<br><br>* Closely monitor patients at higher risk for developing <u>melanoma</u>.<br><br><br> | <br>* Treatment usually not required; if <u>melanoma</u> is suspected, perform a <u>full-thickness excisional biopsy</u>. [[2]](/library/Wk1P5S0)<br><br> | <br>* Complete excision with <u>full-thickness excisional biopsy</u> for histopathological confirmation<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Congenital dermal melanocytosis</u> is a birthmark that manifests as a painless, blue-gray, nonblanching, <u>hyperpigmented</u> <u>macula</u> of the sacral region, and typically disappears in childhood.

### General management of melanocytic nevus [[1]](/library/lPWvUl0)[[2]](/library/Wk1P5S0)




* Melanocytic nevus is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on:

* Complete <u>skin examination</u>

* <u>Dermoscopy</u> as needed

* Perform a <u>full-thickness excisional biopsy</u> if there is suspicion for:

* <u>Melanoma</u> (i.e., <u>ABCDE criteria</u> and/or <u>ugly duckling sign</u>; see also “<u>Diagnostics for melanoma</u>”) [[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)[[5]](/library/Z7WZ450)

* <u>Spitz nevus</u>

* Specific management depends on the type of nevus.

## Common acquired melanocytic nevus

* Definition: an <u>acquired melanocytic nevus</u> that arises from <u>clusters</u> of melanocytic nevus cells in the <u>epidermis</u> and <u>dermis</u> and manifests as a uniformly pigmented lesion [[1]](/library/lPWvUl0)[[2]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: common regardless of age, <u>gender</u>, or ethnicity

* Etiology

* Genetics (parents with many moles)

* Associated with light <u>skin</u> and red <u>hair</u>

* Intense sun exposure during childhood

* Clinical features [[2]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* Most commonly on sun-exposed areas [[1]](/library/lPWvUl0)

* Uniform in color and shape

* Stages [[1]](/library/lPWvUl0)[[2]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* Junctional nevus  

* Uniformly brown-black <u>macule</u> with a flat smooth, hairless surface and well-demarcated border

* Grows at the <u>dermal-epidermal junction</u> during childhood

* Compound nevus  

* Uniformly brown-black, dome-shaped elevated <u>papule</u> or <u>nodule</u> with a smooth or <u>verrucous</u> surface; <u>hair</u> may be present

* Arises from a junctional nevus and extends to the <u>dermis</u> after childhood

* <u>Dermal</u> nevus  

* Uniformly brown-black, dome-shaped elevated <u>nodule</u> with a smooth or <u>verrucous</u> surface; can become <u>fibrotic</u> over time and <u>hair</u> may be present

* Arises from a <u>compound nevus</u> in the <u>dermis</u> in adults

* Management [[1]](/library/lPWvUl0)[[2]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* See “<u>General management of melanocytic nevus</u>.”

* Treatment usually not required unless the patient requests lesion removal for cosmetic reasons

* Prognosis: Transformation to <u>melanoma</u> is rare. [[2]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

## Atypical nevus

<u>Atypical nevus</u> was previously known as <u>dysplastic nevus</u>. [[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)




* Description: a benign melanocytic nevus that resembles <u>melanoma</u> and is a <u>risk factor</u> for developing <u>melanoma</u> [[3]](/library/07We450)[[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: 2–10% in White individuals

* Etiology

* Genetics (parents with many moles)

* Associated with light <u>skin</u>

* Intense sun exposure during childhood

* Clinical features [[3]](/library/07We450)[[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)

* Typically on sun-exposed areas in light <u>skin</u> and non-sun-exposed areas in dark <u>skin</u>

* Appearance is similar to the <u>ABCDE criteria for melanoma</u>: 

* Asymmetry

* Irregular borders

* Color variegation

* Diameter > 5 mm [[3]](/library/07We450)

* Management [[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)[[5]](/library/Z7WZ450)

* See “<u>General management of melanocytic nevus</u>.”

* If <u>melanoma</u> is not currently suspected, monitor with periodic screening.

* Modality: total body <u>skin examination</u> with <u>dermoscopy</u> and/or total body photography

* Frequency: Consider every 3–12 months, depending on <u>risk factors</u>.  [[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)[[5]](/library/Z7WZ450)

* Educate patients to self-monitor for concerning changes in existing nevi.

* Prevention

* Minimize UV radiation exposure (e.g., with <u>photoprotective measures</u>). [[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)[[5]](/library/Z7WZ450)

* See also “<u>Prevention of melanoma</u>.”

* Prognosis

* Lifetime risk of <u>melanoma</u> increases in <u>proportion</u> to the number of <u>atypical nevi</u>. [[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)

* Individuals with familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome (<u>FAMMM</u>) have up to 100% lifetime risk of developing <u>melanoma</u>. [[4]](/library/7FW4jM0)
